meta.scopeStatement: Defines how the approved 120-piece baseline is taught and presented as a sound storybook. It does not replace per-piece score, rights, exact-version, pronunciation, or cultural verification.
meta.expansionStatement: 120 is the floor, not the cap. The architecture supports 200-250+ and 300+ by adding or splitting rooms.

bookArchitecture.productPositioning: A finite, parent-friendly interactive sound storybook that teaches a map of musical culture. It is not a playlist, streaming feed, album shelf, or open-ended recommendation system.

primaryMode.name: Read Together
primaryMode.description: A guided page-turning chapter with a visible beginning, middle, and end. Music is embedded in illustrated scenes and is activated by large sound-book hotspots.
primaryMode.defaultNarration: Parent-read on-screen text. Guide-character voice remains off unless separately approved under audio policy.

returnMode.name: Explore the Room
returnMode.description: After the guided chapter has been completed once, the child may revisit its pieces freely without losing the chapter structure.

knowledgeCoordinates: WHEN: an approximate, overlapping era ribbon rather than a false hard boundary
WHERE: a map anchor and movement route, without claiming one work represents a whole country
WHO: composer, tradition, community, or known adapter
WHAT TO HEAR: one concrete musical cue before abstract vocabulary
WHAT IT CONNECTS TO: an explicit thread to another room, tune family, place, or idea

knowledgeLayers.name: Touch and hear
knowledgeLayers.content: Large sound hotspot, movement, and one visual response.

knowledgeLayers.name: Notice one thing
knowledgeLayers.content: One short listening cue or comparison.

knowledgeLayers.name: Story and connection
knowledgeLayers.content: Two to four lines from the guide characters plus map/timeline context.

knowledgeLayers.name: Parent drawer
knowledgeLayers.content: Nuance, provenance, terms, cautions, and source links.

standardChapterPattern.name: The Doorway
standardChapterPattern.purpose: Opening question, map pin, era ribbon, room thesis, and a visual invitation.

standardChapterPattern.name: Meet the Sounds
standardChapterPattern.purpose: Two or three pieces appear as objects or events inside one continuous scene.

standardChapterPattern.name: Compare and Discover
standardChapterPattern.purpose: Remaining pieces plus one guided A/B comparison, pattern game, or route activity.

standardChapterPattern.name: The Map Bridge
standardChapterPattern.purpose: Place the room on the growing map, reveal one or two connections, and point to the next chapter.

connectionTypes.direct-documented-relationship: Use only when a teacher, student, supporter, collaborator, correspondence, dedication, or other direct link is supported by a source.
connectionTypes.historical-context: People or works shared a city, institution, period, market, or cultural setting; this does not imply personal contact.
connectionTypes.musical-comparison: The app invites the learner to compare audible features; this is an editorial teaching comparison, not a claim of influence.
connectionTypes.shared-tune-family: Two titles or cultural uses share an underlying melody object.
connectionTypes.storybook-sequence: A narrative bridge chosen for learning flow; it is not a historical claim.

parentTrustDesign: Finite chapter route with a visible ending and no infinite feed.
No continuous autoplay; every piece starts from an intentional tap.
No track numbers, album covers, charts, streaks, or recommendation loops.
One educational question per room and one listening idea per piece.
Short child layer; optional adult layer instead of mandatory biography reading.
Music is part of the story scene, not a row of interchangeable play buttons.
Progress means rooms visited and ideas noticed, not minutes watched or points accumulated.
culturalAndHistoricalGuardrails: Era bands overlap. Never imply that a style changed everywhere on one date.
A room may use a place as an anchor, but no single song or composer stands for an entire nation or culture.
Avoid flag collages, costume tourism, generic exotic architecture, and blended fantasy regions.
For traditional and world repertoire, lock the exact melody variant, language, pronunciation, source, and cultural note before final art or score work.
Separate an old melody from later lyrics, arrangements, recordings, anthem uses, and commercial adaptations.
Sacred-origin works may be explained historically and musically without devotional instruction.
Label comparisons as comparisons unless evidence supports influence or a direct relationship.
Do not reduce composers to disability, nationality, tragedy, or one famous anecdote.
bookArchitecture.expansionRule: The baseline 120 is a launch floor, not a ceiling. Add a sibling room or split a chapter when a room exceeds roughly seven or eight core works, requires more than two teaching theses, or would need a scrolling card shelf. Expansion should deepen the map rather than append more records to an overcrowded room.

wings.title: Songs We Already Carry
wings.narrativePurpose: Begin with familiar tunes so the learner discovers that music already has shape, repetition, movement, and memory before meeting formal history.
wings.mapLogic: The map begins close to the child: home, playground, community, and shared song.

wings.title: The World Sings
wings.narrativePurpose: Show that melodies belong to particular languages, places, histories, and uses, while also travelling and changing.
wings.mapLogic: Separate regional rooms connected by visible routes; never one undifferentiated Around the World shelf.

wings.title: Music for Shared Days
wings.narrativePurpose: Examine how communities use songs to mark birthdays, winter, ceremonies, endings, and new beginnings.
wings.mapLogic: Calendar and social-use map rather than a composer map.

wings.title: The Time Corridor
wings.narrativePurpose: Introduce Baroque and Classical sound worlds, then let Beethoven visibly open the door toward Romantic scale and expression.
wings.mapLogic: A west/central European route with overlapping era bands and city anchors.

wings.title: The Romantic Century
wings.narrativePurpose: Show that nineteenth-century music can be private, national, theatrical, pictorial, dance-driven, or story-driven rather than one uniform Romantic sound.
wings.mapLogic: A network of cities and cultural routes rather than a single chronological hallway.

wings.title: Cities, Colour, and a New Pulse
wings.narrativePurpose: End the baseline journey by comparing theatre cities, Parisian sound-colour, American ragtime, and British orchestral modernity.
wings.mapLogic: Same broad era, different places and different musical answers: location and social setting matter.

rooms.title: Melody Detective Workshop
rooms.subtitle: One tune can have a shape, a pattern, and more than one name.
rooms.openingQuestion: How can you recognise a tune even when its words or pictures change?
rooms.thesis: A melody is an organised path of pitches and rhythms. Titles and words may change, but the underlying path can remain recognisable.

era.label: Traditional and eighteenth-to-nineteenth-century tune transmission
era.display: Before recordings -> songs travel through people, print, schools, and homes
era.caution: Do not assign one date to every traditional version.

geography.anchor: A cross-border workshop rather than one national room
geography.mapTreatment: Name the documented or likely source context of each exact version; show routes only after verification.

rooms.setting: A warm inventor workshop where coloured melody ribbons pass through magnifying glasses, gears, bridges, and music boxes. The same ribbon can wear different title tags.
narrativeArc: The guides find three labels attached to one melody ribbon.
They learn to follow direction: up, down, repeat, pause, and surprise.
A second melody enters before the first has finished, introducing a round.
The child leaves with a detective card: listen for shape before reading the title.
learningGoals: Separate a melody from its title and lyrics.
Notice melodic contour and repetition.
Understand a tune family as one musical object with several cultural uses.
Experience a simple round without requiring notation knowledge.
rooms.soundBookMechanic: Large physical-looking tabs change the label attached to a melody ribbon. A second tap overlays a contour trace; no notation is required.

pieces.sceneRole: Three title plaques rotate above one glowing melody ribbon; every plaque activates the same base tune.
pieces.teachingUse: Establish the central tune-family idea and later link to Mozart variation technique.

pieces.sceneRole: Two guide characters walk the same circular path, with the second starting later.
pieces.teachingUse: Introduce a round as the same melody entering at different times.

pieces.sceneRole: A bridge of note-blocks slopes and drops as the phrase moves.
pieces.teachingUse: Make melodic direction visible and show that a familiar tune can be recognised from contour.

pieces.sceneRole: A wind-up box turns through the phrase and opens on the final musical surprise.
pieces.teachingUse: Show expectation, tension, and a sudden release without formal theory language.

pieces.sceneRole: Three small lights descend the first steps together, then travel through the rest of the phrase.
pieces.teachingUse: Give the child a clean example of a descending opening shape.

compareActivity.prompt: Which two tunes begin by moving down? Which one saves its surprise for the end?
compareActivity.interaction: Drag transparent contour ribbons over one another; the app says same direction, different rhythm rather than right/wrong.

connections.label: The familiar Twinkle-family tune later becomes material for Mozart variations.
After finding melody shapes, notice how repeated sections let groups join in.

parentLayer: A tune family is not several separate catalogue counts.
The French title attached to Mozart is not proof that every modern nursery version has one simple origin story.
The app should distinguish the traditional base melody from Mozart K.265 as a separate composed work.

artDirection.palette: honey wood, teal, coral, soft brass

expansion.futureRoomIdea: If the collection grows, split out a dedicated Tune Families and Borrowed Melodies room.
expansion.splitTrigger: More than seven core examples or more than three tune families.

rooms.title: Playground of Patterns
rooms.subtitle: Songs become easy to join when something comes back.
rooms.openingQuestion: Why can a whole group sing some songs after hearing only one verse?
rooms.thesis: Repetition, call-and-response, lists, and returning refrains make community songs learnable and participatory.

era.label: Traditional community and childhood repertoire
era.display: Songs learned through play, family, school, and social repetition
era.caution: Exact words and melodies vary by place and generation.

geography.anchor: Community play rather than a single country
geography.mapTreatment: Use small source tags per tune; do not merge all English-language songs into one origin.

rooms.setting: A living playground where paths loop, animals answer signs, letters light up, and a circular dance returns to its starting point.
narrativeArc: The guides try to remember a long song and discover that the refrain helps.
Each playground station reveals a different kind of repetition.
The child assembles a group performance by activating recurring parts.
The exit shows that repeated patterns are tools used far beyond children's music.
learningGoals: Recognise a refrain and recurring section.
Notice call-and-response and cumulative structure.
Understand that repetition can invite participation rather than signal simplicity.
Prepare for repeated basses, motifs, and variations in later rooms.
rooms.soundBookMechanic: Every hotspot adds one recurring layer to a playground loop. The loop stops at the end of the spread and never becomes background autoplay.

pieces.sceneRole: Boats travel around a short river loop; a second boat can enter later after the first version is heard alone.
pieces.teachingUse: Reinforce round/canon behaviour in a participatory setting.

pieces.sceneRole: Farm gates reveal a stable refrain with one changing animal window.
pieces.teachingUse: Show fixed musical frame plus replaceable verse content.

pieces.sceneRole: Five letter-lanterns switch from sung name to clap one at a time.
pieces.teachingUse: Let the child experience substitution inside a repeated pattern.

pieces.sceneRole: A circular path adds and changes characters while the tune returns.
pieces.teachingUse: Show social chain and recurring structure without claiming one definitive lyric order.

pieces.sceneRole: A ring path changes its action pictures while retaining the same musical frame.
pieces.teachingUse: Connect repetition to movement and everyday actions.
pieces.canonicalTitle: Here We Go Round the Mulberry Bush

compareActivity.prompt: What stays the same, and what changes?
compareActivity.interaction: The child places a gold frame around the recurring part and movable picture cards over the changing part.

connections.label: A repeating frame in a play song can prepare the ear for repeating basses and patterns in Baroque music.
Once a group can join the pattern, the next question is how the beat helps bodies move together.

parentLayer: Traditional repertoire requires exact-variant records rather than a single universal lyric.
The activity should not score singing accuracy; it teaches structural noticing.
Group participation is the educational purpose, not a karaoke mode.

artDirection.palette: spring green, sky blue, red accents, chalk white

expansion.futureRoomIdea: A later Hands, Claps, and Action Songs room can hold more embodied repertoire.
expansion.splitTrigger: When action songs and cumulative songs each need their own teaching thesis.

rooms.title: Steps, Beats, and Marches
rooms.subtitle: The beat is the floor that music walks on.
rooms.openingQuestion: What makes one tune feel like a careful step, another like a dance, and another like a parade?
rooms.thesis: A steady pulse supports many kinds of movement, while rhythm changes the character of those steps.

era.label: Traditional and community repertoire
era.display: Simple teaching tunes -> dances -> processional songs
era.caution: Do not flatten distinct performance traditions into one universal march beat.

geography.anchor: Movement routes across community traditions
geography.mapTreatment: Treat When the Saints with specific cultural context and avoid generic parade imagery detached from its history.

rooms.setting: A long illustrated street changes from stepping stones to market dance floor to a community procession. Each song activates a different pattern of footprints.
narrativeArc: The guides find a glowing floor pulse.
A three-note tune shows that few pitches can still organise clear rhythm.
Dance steps loosen the path.
The final procession gathers people without turning the room into spectacle.
learningGoals: Feel steady pulse separately from melody.
Compare sparse pitch material with richer rhythmic identity.
Notice dance versus processional character.
Use body movement as a listening tool, not a performance test.
rooms.soundBookMechanic: Tapping a footprint starts one short phrase; soft floor lights mark pulse while larger character movements show rhythm. Playback ends after the phrase.

pieces.sceneRole: A lamb crosses three nearby stepping stones and returns.
pieces.teachingUse: Show how a small pitch range can create a highly recognisable tune.

pieces.sceneRole: Three bakery bells use only a tiny set of pitches with a distinct rhythm.
pieces.teachingUse: Compare minimal pitch material and rhythm with Mary Had a Little Lamb.

pieces.sceneRole: Numbered tokens bounce on recurring beat points, with the phrase returning after each verse.
pieces.teachingUse: Connect counting, pulse, and refrain without turning the room into a maths exercise.

pieces.sceneRole: Paired footprints cross and turn on a dance floor.
pieces.teachingUse: Introduce social dance energy and repeated movement cues.

pieces.sceneRole: A respectful community procession advances along the street as the strong pulse becomes visible.
pieces.teachingUse: Introduce a processional song with cultural context and a clear forward-moving beat.
pieces.canonicalTitle: When the Saints Go Marching In

compareActivity.prompt: Can you keep the floor pulse while the tune changes above it?
compareActivity.interaction: Hold one large pulse pad while tapping the visible rhythm lights with the other hand; no speed score.

connections.label: Processional and celebration songs both organise groups, but their social uses and histories differ.
Later, waltz, polka, habanera, and overture will show more specialised movement styles.

parentLayer: Explain pulse as the recurring underlying beat; do not imply every performance uses identical tempo or accompaniment.
When the Saints needs specific historical and community context in the parent drawer before publication.
No motion tracking or dance scoring is required.

artDirection.palette: terracotta, cream, deep blue, warm street-lamp gold

expansion.futureRoomIdea: A later Dance Map can compare metre and social dance forms across eras.
expansion.splitTrigger: When the room includes more than two distinct culturally specific processional traditions.

rooms.title: Home, Distance, and Belonging
rooms.subtitle: Some tunes hold a person, a memory, or a faraway place.
rooms.openingQuestion: How can a simple melody make people think of home, comfort, distance, or hope?
rooms.thesis: Familiar songs often carry social memory. Their meaning comes from use, words, community, and history as well as notes.

era.label: Traditional and nineteenth-century song traditions
era.display: Cradle -> meeting place -> journey -> imagined home
era.caution: Meaning changes across communities and later uses.

geography.anchor: Transatlantic routes and North American landscapes
geography.mapTreatment: Use route lines and source labels; never present a generic old-time America as one culture.

rooms.setting: A twilight house opens into a road, a ship horizon, a meeting room, and a wide landscape. One continuous ribbon of light links comfort to distance.
narrativeArc: The room begins beside a cradle with a rocking phrase.
The door opens to community and spiritual song.
A path and ship carry melodies away from home.
The guides place each song on a memory map rather than ranking which is happiest or saddest.
learningGoals: Hear rocking, spacious, and hymn-like phrase shapes.
Understand that musical meaning is partly social and historical.
Compare home as a physical place with home as remembered or hoped for.
Prepare for Romantic themes of memory, longing, and identity.
rooms.soundBookMechanic: The child opens scene windows rather than selecting tracks. Each window plays one bounded excerpt and reveals one sentence about use or meaning.

pieces.sceneRole: A cradle gently rocks in time with the phrase, then rests.
pieces.teachingUse: Introduce lullaby motion and the idea of music used for care.

pieces.sceneRole: A plain meeting-room window glows as the tune unfolds without showy staging.
pieces.teachingUse: Introduce a melody whose cultural life depends on text, community, and later history; keep the exact New Britain tune explicit.

pieces.sceneRole: A simple wooden path turns and returns to its starting point.
pieces.teachingUse: Connect musical simplicity, community use, and a tune that later travelled into other works.

pieces.sceneRole: A small boat and distant light make the separation in the song visible.
pieces.teachingUse: Use long distance and return as an emotional listening frame.
pieces.canonicalTitle: My Bonnie Lies over the Ocean

pieces.sceneRole: A broad horizon slowly opens behind the melody.
pieces.teachingUse: Show how spacious visual framing can support a song associated with landscape and home.
pieces.creatorOrTradition: Daniel E. Kelley / Brewster M. Higley; historical song

compareActivity.prompt: Which tune rocks, which travels, and which opens a wide space?
compareActivity.interaction: Choose one of three motion cards - rock, travel, open - and see that more than one answer can be discussed.

connections.label: Later, Brahms and Dvorak turn lullaby, memory, dance, and place into composed concert music.
Lullaby-like softness also appears in seasonal and sacred repertoire.

parentLayer: Do not treat historical community songs as neutral aesthetic objects; contextual notes must be reviewed.
Use the exact New Britain melody record for Amazing Grace.
The child layer should invite feeling without assigning one compulsory emotion.

artDirection.palette: indigo dusk, warm amber, muted sage, moonlit blue

expansion.futureRoomIdea: Split into Lullabies and Songs of Home/Journey when the traditional library expands.
expansion.splitTrigger: More than two lullabies or more than four place-and-memory songs.

rooms.title: Gardens of Season and Memory
rooms.subtitle: Three familiar songs, three places, and three different cultural lives.
rooms.openingQuestion: Can songs about flowers, seasons, and memory sound connected without being treated as the same tradition?
rooms.thesis: Nearby regions can share broad musical resources while maintaining distinct languages, histories, variants, and social meanings.

era.label: Traditional and historically transmitted repertoire
era.display: Exact dates vary by song and version
era.caution: Do not present a single timeless East Asian style.

geography.anchor: Three separate garden pavilions
geography.mapTreatment: Give each pavilion its own local name, script, pronunciation, source note, and map pin; connect only through explicit comparison lines.

rooms.setting: A triptych garden seen from one path: cherry blossom viewing, a mountain-road memory landscape, and a jasmine courtyard. Architectural and botanical details remain place-specific.
narrativeArc: The guides receive three flower or memory tokens that look similar from far away.
Each pavilion reveals a distinct melody and cultural context.
The child compares phrase shape and tonal material without being told that one scale explains a region.
The map bridge states: neighbours can sound related in some ways and different in others.
learningGoals: Associate each tune with its own place and name.
Compare melodic shape without cultural flattening.
Understand that a traditional song may have many variants.
Learn that geographic proximity does not erase difference.
rooms.soundBookMechanic: Three large garden objects activate one verified verse or phrase each. A compare lens can highlight recurring pitch sets only after the tunes are heard normally.

pieces.sceneRole: A branch opens blossom by blossom along the phrase.
pieces.teachingUse: Anchor a Japanese seasonal song while making the exact selected variant explicit.

pieces.sceneRole: A path crosses a low ridge and returns toward a distant lantern.
pieces.teachingUse: Present one named regional/standard variant and connect melody to memory and journey without claiming one definitive Arirang.

pieces.sceneRole: Jasmine flowers open in balanced phrase groups around a courtyard.
pieces.teachingUse: Anchor a Chinese song tradition and invite comparison of contour and repetition with Sakura Sakura.

compareActivity.prompt: What do you notice about repetition, gaps, and the way each melody turns?
compareActivity.interaction: A slow visual trace follows each phrase; the guides model observation language rather than declaring one song representative of a country.

connections.label: Continue south through distinct language and musical communities rather than entering one generic world-music room.
Later, compare how composed concert works also evoke season, atmosphere, and image.

parentLayer: Exact variant, language, transliteration, pronunciation, and source are release gates.
Avoid claiming that pentatonic material is unique to or universal across these traditions.
Commission cultural review of text, art, and naming before publication.

artDirection.palette: three coordinated but distinct palettes; no single regional wash

expansion.futureRoomIdea: Add sibling rooms for Japanese childhood songs, Korean regional Arirang variants, and Chinese regional song traditions only with reviewed sources.
expansion.splitTrigger: Any addition that would require representing more than one major tradition per country inside the same three-song chapter.

rooms.title: Southeast Asian Courtyard
rooms.subtitle: Songs travel across islands, languages, courts, homes, and schools.
rooms.openingQuestion: What changes when songs travel by sea, by family, by school, or through a court tradition?
rooms.thesis: Southeast Asia is not one musical style. A map can reveal proximity and routes while each song keeps its own language, setting, and history.

era.label: Traditional and historical song transmission
era.display: Multiple timelines shown side by side
era.caution: Do not force all four songs into one date or origin story.

geography.anchor: A connected sea-and-mainland map with four distinct listening courtyards
geography.mapTreatment: Use sea routes and local anchors as orientation, not as claims of direct influence unless verified.

rooms.setting: A broad coastal courtyard opens to four clearly separated spaces: a social singing veranda, a bird-story corner, a garden-game path, and a moonlit Thai pavilion.
narrativeArc: The guides unfold a map that seems close geographically but contains several languages and song uses.
Two lively social songs open the courtyard.
A Philippine game/story song adds another community context.
The room quiets at the Thai pavilion, showing contrast inside the region rather than a single regional sound.
learningGoals: Map four repertoire objects to specific places and languages.
Hear contrast between social/playful and lyrical/court-associated presentation.
Understand that travel routes are hypotheses unless documented.
Practice respectful comparison without ranking authenticity.
rooms.soundBookMechanic: A fold-out map opens four scene panels. Each piece is activated in its own panel; a route overlay is optional and never plays songs as a continuous medley.

pieces.sceneRole: A veranda exchange lights alternating response lanterns.
pieces.teachingUse: Introduce a social song with language and regional-use notes, avoiding one-country ownership claims where history is shared or debated.

pieces.sceneRole: A cockatoo illustration reacts to recurring phrases in a story corner.
pieces.teachingUse: Use character and repetition while preserving the song's specific language and source context.

pieces.sceneRole: Garden objects move along a game-like path as the phrase unfolds.
pieces.teachingUse: Represent a Philippine childhood/community song through action rather than costume.

pieces.sceneRole: A moon reflection and measured pavilion movement accompany the melody.
pieces.teachingUse: Introduce a Thai composed/historical song as a distinct lyrical tradition, not generic folk background.
pieces.creatorOrTradition: Prince Benbadhanabongse / Thai classical song tradition

compareActivity.prompt: Which songs invite a group action, and which asks the room to become still?
compareActivity.interaction: The child places each song on a spectrum from join-in to listen-closely, with an explanation that use depends on context.

connections.label: The map now follows songs that travelled through trade, pilgrimage, city life, and migration.
Lao Duang Duen and other lyrical songs can be compared around longing and memory without claiming shared origin.

parentLayer: All four entries require exact version, language, pronunciation, and cultural-review records.
Do not decorate with a blended temple, tropical, or costume aesthetic.
Where ownership or origin is contested, state the uncertainty and show multiple legitimate associations.

artDirection.palette: coastal turquoise, leaf green, woven neutrals, moonlit violet; distinct panel accents

expansion.futureRoomIdea: Add country- or tradition-specific sibling rooms after reviewed repertoire reaches critical mass.
expansion.splitTrigger: More than one additional song for any represented place, or any need for deeper instrument-specific teaching.

rooms.title: Roads of Prayer, City, and Sea
rooms.subtitle: A melody can cross borders and collect new uses without losing its history.
rooms.openingQuestion: When a song travels, what stays recognisable and what changes?
rooms.thesis: Songs may move through religious practice, urban life, trade routes, migration, print, theatre, and recording. The app must distinguish documented history from an attractive travel story.

era.label: Historical and traditional repertoire with later adaptations
era.display: Older roots -> named versions -> modern circulation
era.caution: Exact lineage differs by song; do not draw a route without evidence.

geography.anchor: Three separate route tables
geography.mapTreatment: Each song gets its own route and source card. Routes never merge into a generic Silk Road narrative.

rooms.setting: A quiet map room with three windows: a processional path, an Istanbul street and ferry, and a Mediterranean harbour. The guides use route cards marked known, possible, or later adaptation.
narrativeArc: The guides discover that a map line can be a fact, a possibility, or merely an illustration.
The first song is presented in a sacred/social context without devotional instruction.
The second places melody inside city life and a named language.
The third reveals multiple regional versions and later performance identities.
learningGoals: Separate musical travel from unverified origin stories.
Respect sacred and community uses while focusing on musical learning.
Recognise that one melody may have several regional versions.
Use evidence labels when describing cultural transmission.
rooms.soundBookMechanic: A route appears only after the child taps an evidence card. Sound buttons live inside place-specific scenes and never trigger a cross-cultural mash-up.

pieces.sceneRole: A measured path of lamps follows the selected phrase while a context drawer identifies language, use, and exact version.
pieces.teachingUse: Model respectful presentation of a song with religious and civic associations without turning the room into worship or generic Indian imagery.

pieces.sceneRole: Street signs and ferry windows reveal the melody in an Istanbul city scene.
pieces.teachingUse: Show how a song can belong to urban memory and circulate under more than one title or spelling.

pieces.sceneRole: Separate harbour radios reveal documented regional versions only after the base melody is heard.
pieces.teachingUse: Teach that the famous modern instrumental identity is a later arrangement layer, not the whole history of the melody.

compareActivity.prompt: Which information belongs to the melody, and which belongs to one later performance?
compareActivity.interaction: Sort cards into melody, words/title, arrangement, recording, and later use. The app accepts unknown when evidence is incomplete.

connections.label: The next room focuses on tunes whose later identities became almost as famous as their earlier forms.
Later theatre and publishing networks also move dances and melodies between cities.

parentLayer: Every route claim needs a source and evidence label.
Religious context should be accurate, brief, and non-devotional.
Misirlou must use a documented historical melody and an original transcription, not the surf-rock arrangement.

artDirection.palette: sandstone, deep sea blue, saffron accents, evening teal

expansion.futureRoomIdea: A later Melodies in Motion wing can hold additional well-documented migration and trade-route case studies.
expansion.splitTrigger: Any new song requires a route unrelated to the three existing histories.

rooms.title: Songs That Transform
rooms.subtitle: A tune can become a dance, a celebration, a carol, or a symbol.
rooms.openingQuestion: Is a song still the same song after people give it new words, a new setting, or a new social purpose?
rooms.thesis: Musical identity has layers: base melody, named composer or adapter, lyrics, arrangement, performance practice, and later cultural use.

era.label: Nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century layers over older or folk materials
era.display: Source layer -> named shaping -> later public identity
era.caution: Do not label all four works simply traditional.

geography.anchor: Four transformation cabinets
geography.mapTreatment: Each cabinet has a creator/tradition field and a later-use field; country labels do not replace those distinctions.

rooms.setting: A transformation gallery where the same melody sheet passes through dance shoes, a choral lantern, new lyric pages, and public celebration scenes.
narrativeArc: The guides first hear each melody without its most familiar modern image.
They open drawers for composer/adapter, words, arrangement, and later use.
They discover that known authorship and folk circulation can coexist.
The exit gives the child four layer badges to use throughout the rest of the book.
learningGoals: Distinguish melody from lyrics and arrangement.
Understand that folk-like popularity does not always mean anonymous authorship.
Recognise later seasonal or national use as a layer, not an origin.
Prepare for tune reuse and variation in composed music.
rooms.soundBookMechanic: A base-melody button plays first. Additional visual layers may be revealed, but the app never substitutes a copyrighted later arrangement for the verified source melody.

pieces.sceneRole: A celebration circle appears only after the melody and historical context card are introduced.
pieces.teachingUse: Show how a melody can become widely associated with celebration while retaining specific cultural history.

pieces.sceneRole: A printed song page opens into a later folk-stage scene, with a clear known-creator field.
pieces.teachingUse: Correct the common assumption that every folk-like national favourite is anonymous.

pieces.sceneRole: A Ukrainian choral pattern turns through repeating cells; a separate locked drawer labels later English carol identity.
pieces.teachingUse: Teach base work versus later lyrics and seasonal adaptation.

pieces.sceneRole: An old melody page receives a later lyric overlay that can be lifted away.
pieces.teachingUse: Demonstrate how one tune supports different textual and seasonal identities.

compareActivity.prompt: Which layer changed: the tune, the words, the setting, or the public meaning?
compareActivity.interaction: Stack transparent cards over each melody. Only historically supported cards can be attached.

connections.label: Shchedryk and Greensleeves connect to later seasonal uses without becoming duplicate tune records.
Mozart variations transform one tune inside a composed work; this room transforms tunes through social history.

parentLayer: Kalinka has known authorship and should not be presented as anonymous.
Shchedryk and the later English Carol of the Bells layer require separate metadata.
For Hava Nagila, lock the exact melody history and named shaping/adapter record before publication.
Greensleeves and What Child Is This must remain one tune-family object with distinct text/use layers.

artDirection.palette: deep plum, forest green, gold paper, winter blue

expansion.futureRoomIdea: A dedicated Borrowed Tunes and New Words room can absorb more tune-family cases.
expansion.splitTrigger: More than six works or more than two later-use layers per work.

rooms.title: When a Song Means Home
rooms.subtitle: Some melodies grow into public symbols, but they began in particular histories.
rooms.openingQuestion: How does a song become connected with a place, a people, or a shared memory?
rooms.thesis: A song may become a civic, national, regional, or diasporic symbol through repeated public use. That later role should not erase its composer, local tradition, or earlier form.

era.label: Late nineteenth to early twentieth century, with traditional roots in some cases
era.display: Creation or tradition -> circulation -> public symbol
era.caution: Symbolic status varies by community and time.

geography.anchor: Four home-map cases
geography.mapTreatment: Use four independent map panels and a shared question; never imply equivalent political histories.

rooms.setting: A map hall where each panel begins as a small local scene and gradually expands to show later public circulation, migration, or adaptation.
narrativeArc: The guides ask whether a famous public song always began as an anthem.
Each panel reveals a different path from local work or tradition to wider identity.
The child hears base melodies before later public associations are explained.
The wing closes with a reminder: a map pin is a beginning for learning, not a label that captures a whole culture.
learningGoals: Understand that songs can acquire civic or national meaning over time.
Preserve known creators and local forms.
Distinguish traditional melody from later popular arrangement.
Compare social function without equating historical experiences.
rooms.soundBookMechanic: Each map panel has two stages: hear the source melody, then open a context window showing later public use. No flags animate during playback.

pieces.sceneRole: A small school/community singing scene expands into a carefully sourced public-history panel.
pieces.teachingUse: Teach that a composed song can later carry major civic and anthem significance.
pieces.creatorOrTradition: Enoch Sontonga / Southern African hymn tradition

pieces.sceneRole: A travelling story map follows selected lyric imagery while the exact historical tune version remains named.
pieces.teachingUse: Show how a song becomes strongly associated with a place without calling it an official anthem.

pieces.sceneRole: A theatre manuscript opens first, followed by later Andean and international circulation layers.
pieces.teachingUse: Preserve the original composed-work context and separate it from famous later arrangements.

pieces.sceneRole: A Veracruz dance platform presents the traditional son jarocho identity before a later pop-history drawer.
pieces.teachingUse: Distinguish living regional tradition from a twentieth-century commercial arrangement.

compareActivity.prompt: Did this begin as a public symbol, or did public meaning grow later?
compareActivity.interaction: Place each story card on a three-step path: source context, wider circulation, later public identity. Unknown details remain visibly open.

connections.label: The next wing asks how songs mark shared times and ceremonies without necessarily representing a nation.
Dvorak also wrote about place and identity in concert music, but through a different medium and historical situation.

parentLayer: Nkosi Sikelel iAfrika, Waltzing Matilda, El Condor Pasa, and La Bamba each require creator/version and cultural review.
Do not use national flag triumphalism or imply identical relationships between song and state.
Original composition, traditional performance, later lyrics, and popular recording must remain separate rights and metadata objects.

artDirection.palette: four locally grounded palettes joined by neutral map parchment
avoid: tourist landmarks as the only identifiers

expansion.futureRoomIdea: Add new public-symbol case studies only when the project can support local scholarly/cultural review.
expansion.splitTrigger: More than four core cases; each deserves enough space for its distinct history.

rooms.title: Celebration Square
rooms.subtitle: People use songs to begin, gather, congratulate, and say goodbye.
rooms.openingQuestion: Why do certain tunes appear whenever people share an important moment?
rooms.thesis: Function shapes musical memory: a short singable tune can become attached to birthdays, congratulations, winter gatherings, worship, or year-end reflection.

era.label: Eighteenth- and nineteenth-century tunes with later social uses
era.display: Tune history and modern occasion shown as separate layers
era.caution: Current use is not always the original use.

geography.anchor: A social-use square with source-route drawers
geography.mapTreatment: Occasion icons lead; historical source places remain visible in the adult layer.

rooms.setting: A town square changes through five bounded moments: birthday table, congratulations arch, winter sleigh path, communal singing steps, and year-turning clock.
narrativeArc: The guides arrive before an event and must choose music for its purpose.
They learn that a tune's present occasion may be later than its origin.
A shared-tune case reveals one melody under different texts.
The chapter ends at a clock, connecting celebration with memory and endings.
learningGoals: Identify music by social function as well as composer/place.
Understand that current occasion and origin can differ.
Recognise shared tune families.
Compare group singing with listening-only concert repertoire.
rooms.soundBookMechanic: The child places an occasion object in the square; one suitable song appears with a short context line. There is no shuffle or party playlist.

pieces.sceneRole: Candles light one phrase at a time around a single birthday scene.
pieces.teachingUse: Use the most familiar occasion song to introduce social function and global later circulation.
pieces.creatorOrTradition: Patty Hill and Mildred J. Hill / historical birthday song

pieces.sceneRole: A congratulations arch flips to reveal the Bear Went Over the Mountain alternate-title layer.
pieces.teachingUse: Reinforce tune-family logic inside a social-use context.
pieces.canonicalTitle: For He's a Jolly Good Fellow

pieces.sceneRole: A sleigh route appears as a winter social song, with a parent note separating present Christmas use from early context.
pieces.teachingUse: Show how seasonal association can grow over time.

pieces.sceneRole: Broad communal steps illuminate with the strong phrase, with sacred origin noted but not taught devotionally.
pieces.teachingUse: Include a widely recognised communal seasonal/hymn tune and compare large public singing with intimate lullaby.
pieces.creatorOrTradition: Lowell Mason setting / Isaac Watts text lineage

pieces.sceneRole: A year-turning clock opens memory windows to people and places.
pieces.teachingUse: Connect music with farewell, continuity, and shared remembrance.

compareActivity.prompt: Which song fits beginning, congratulating, gathering, or remembering - and why?
compareActivity.interaction: Match occasion cards, then open a historical note showing that use and origin are different questions.

connections.label: Move from a mixed celebration square into one quieter seasonal chapter with several different musical functions.
Ode to Joy also became a public communal melody, but it began inside a large symphonic work.

parentLayer: Avoid claiming that present-day seasonal use was always the original use.
Sacred-origin items should be framed historically and musically.
Use one tune-family record where melodies are shared; occasions are presentation layers, not duplicate songs.

artDirection.palette: warm civic gold, winter blue, berry red, clock-face cream

expansion.futureRoomIdea: A later Ceremonies and Public Music room can separate graduation, procession, and formal civic uses.
expansion.splitTrigger: More than six occasion types or any need to add national/official ceremonial repertoire.

rooms.title: Winter Lanterns
rooms.subtitle: One season can hold lullaby, evergreen, dance, visiting, and story.
rooms.openingQuestion: Why do winter songs sound so different even when people hear them in the same season?
rooms.thesis: A seasonal collection is not one musical style. Songs enter it through sacred story, lullaby, older dance tune, visiting custom, and later reuse.

era.label: Traditional and eighteenth-to-nineteenth-century song layers
era.display: Different origins gathered into one later seasonal repertoire
era.caution: Do not present Christmas repertoire as universal or culturally neutral.

geography.anchor: Five lantern windows with separate origin cards
geography.mapTreatment: A calendar frame may gather the songs, but each retains its own source place and use.

rooms.setting: A quiet winter street with five lantern windows: cradle, evergreen, dance hall, visiting doorway, and star/story window. No shopping imagery.
narrativeArc: The square becomes quiet after celebration.
Each lantern reveals a different reason a song belongs to the season.
The guides compare soft rocking, dance motion, and visiting refrain.
The wing closes by separating shared season from shared origin.
learningGoals: Hear multiple functions inside one seasonal category.
Separate tune from later translated text or seasonal use.
Compare lullaby, dance, visiting, and narrative song.
Understand that collections are editorial groupings, not historical proof of one style.
rooms.soundBookMechanic: Each lantern plays one short excerpt and reveals a single origin/use icon. The page has a fixed end; there is no looping holiday ambience.

pieces.sceneRole: A cradle-like lantern breathes slowly with the phrase.
pieces.teachingUse: Present quiet, rocking seasonal music and sacred origin with restrained context.

pieces.sceneRole: An evergreen lantern switches between older tree-song context and later seasonal text layers.
pieces.teachingUse: Reinforce that familiar seasonal words can be one layer over an older tune history.

pieces.sceneRole: A Welsh dance-pattern lantern moves before the later English seasonal text drawer opens.
pieces.teachingUse: Show dance-tune origin and later seasonal reuse.

pieces.sceneRole: A doorway scene shows visiting and reciprocal singing rather than a stage performance.
pieces.teachingUse: Introduce song as social custom and group exchange.
pieces.canonicalTitle: We Wish You a Merry Christmas

pieces.sceneRole: A story lantern reveals phrase sections one at a time.
pieces.teachingUse: Represent narrative carol function without requiring doctrinal instruction.

compareActivity.prompt: Which lantern rocks, which dances, which visits, and which tells a story?
compareActivity.interaction: Place function symbols beneath the lanterns; the parent drawer explains that functions may overlap.

connections.label: Greensleeves and Shchedryk connect to later seasonal identities without duplicate melody objects.
The next wing leaves the calendar and enters a time corridor where musical construction becomes visible.

parentLayer: This room should be optional or neutrally labelled for families who do not observe Christmas.
Sacred texts are contextual; the core interaction concerns musical function and history.
Translated titles and later lyrics require separate metadata from the tune.

artDirection.palette: deep navy, warm lantern amber, evergreen, soft snow white

expansion.futureRoomIdea: Create sibling seasonal rooms for other calendars only with sufficient, culturally reviewed repertoire and without forcing equivalence.
expansion.splitTrigger: More than one additional cultural calendar or more than seven winter pieces.

rooms.title: Baroque Pattern Workshop
rooms.subtitle: Lines repeat, overlap, and build a larger design.
rooms.openingQuestion: How can repeating shapes and independent lines make music feel as if it is always moving?
rooms.thesis: Much Baroque music creates momentum through recurring basses, sequences, arpeggiated patterns, and lines that fit together. The room teaches construction before biography.

era.label: Baroque
era.display: Approximately 1600-1750, shown as an overlapping teaching band
era.caution: The date band is a guide, not a simultaneous global style change.

geography.anchor: German-speaking central Europe
places: Nuremberg region and wider German-speaking courts/churches
geography.mapTreatment: Use composer-specific pins rather than one Baroque nation.

rooms.setting: A giant musical clockwork workshop where independent ribbons, stairs, arches, and bass wheels combine into one moving structure.
narrativeArc: The guides enter after learning repetition in play songs.
A keyboard pattern becomes a staircase of harmony.
A long singing line floats above steady movement.
A repeating bass wheel supports a canon, proving that pattern can create architecture rather than boredom.
learningGoals: Hear recurring pattern, sequence, bass support, and independent line.
Distinguish repetition of a frame from repetition of a whole tune.
Place Bach and Pachelbel before the Classical-era rooms on the timeline.
Prepare for Baroque public spectacle in the next room.
rooms.soundBookMechanic: Each piece activates a different transparent mechanism. The child can isolate one line, then hear lines together; the default view remains pictorial rather than score-heavy.

pieces.sceneRole: A staircase of broken chords rises through the workshop.
pieces.teachingUse: Show how a repeating keyboard pattern can support changing harmony; retain patterned texture rather than a bare melody.

pieces.sceneRole: A long ribbon floats over slowly moving support gears.
pieces.teachingUse: Contrast sustained melodic line with the workshop's busier repeated motion.
pieces.canonicalTitle: Air from Orchestral Suite No. 3, BWV 1068

pieces.sceneRole: A flowing accompaniment path continues beneath a chorale-like upper line.
pieces.teachingUse: Let the child hear two roles at once and avoid reducing the work to one tune.
pieces.canonicalTitle: Jesu, Joy of Man's Desiring, BWV 147

pieces.sceneRole: One cello-coloured line outlines rooms and arches without accompaniment.
pieces.teachingUse: Show that a single instrument can imply harmony through a continuous line.

pieces.sceneRole: A bass wheel repeats while new melodic ribbons enter and accumulate.
pieces.teachingUse: Provide the clearest room example of repeated bass plus imitative/canonic growth; multi-track representation is required.

compareActivity.prompt: What is repeating: the bass, the surface pattern, the whole tune, or the entry of a new line?
compareActivity.interaction: Turn one mechanism at a time, then combine it. Labels describe audible role, not advanced notation.

connections.label: Both rooms use repetition, but Baroque works build longer structures from overlapping musical roles.
The workshop doors open onto public stages, outdoor spectacle, and musical scene-painting.
The next era keeps inherited craft but favours different balances, forms, and conversational clarity.

parentLayer: Representation mode is a content requirement: texture-dependent works cannot be flattened to a single note line.
The room teaches audible devices, not a universal definition of all Baroque music.
Attribution questions for the reserve Toccata and Fugue must remain visible if added.

artDirection.palette: dark wood, parchment, brass, lapis blue, warm ivory

expansion.futureRoomIdea: Split keyboard/solo pattern from counterpoint and canon if Bach repertoire expands.
expansion.splitTrigger: More than seven core works or more than three texture types requiring separate interactions.

rooms.title: Baroque Stage: Seasons, Water, and Fireworks
rooms.subtitle: Music moves from workshop patterns into weather, ceremony, and public spectacle.
rooms.openingQuestion: How can instruments suggest spring, a storm, cold wind, water, or fireworks without showing a picture?
rooms.thesis: Baroque composers could use recurring musical ideas, contrast, rhythm, and instrumental colour to suggest scenes and organise large public occasions.

era.label: Late Baroque
era.display: Early eighteenth century
era.caution: Vivaldi and Handel are compared as contemporaries in different cities and careers, not as one national style.

geography.anchor: Venice and London connected by a European route
places: Handel's German origins shown in adult layer
geography.mapTreatment: Two city stages remain visually distinct; route indicates career movement only where documented.

rooms.setting: A theatre boat travels from a Venetian seasonal stage to London river and fireworks terraces. Weather mechanisms and public architecture share the same chapter but not one blended city.
narrativeArc: The workshop mechanisms become wind, birds, heat, and storm on a stage.
Three Vivaldi scenes teach recurring solo/orchestra contrast through weather and season.
The boat arrives at London, where music serves royal and public outdoor occasions.
The child compares scene-painting with ceremonial function.
learningGoals: Hear contrast between solo-like foreground and ensemble response.
Connect tempo, articulation, register, and repetition with suggested scene or motion.
Differentiate descriptive/programmatic cue from ceremonial social function.
Locate Venice and London within the same era but different musical settings.
rooms.soundBookMechanic: Scene objects trigger short paired excerpts or motifs: foreground gesture first, response second. Weather effects are visual only; no added thunder samples obscure the music.

pieces.sceneRole: Bird-like ribbons and a flowing brook appear as recurring musical gestures on a Venetian stage.
pieces.teachingUse: Introduce scene association and solo/ensemble contrast through a highly recognisable movement.
pieces.canonicalTitle: The Four Seasons - Spring, first movement

pieces.sceneRole: Clouds accumulate as rapid figures and forceful returns cross the stage.
pieces.teachingUse: Show how speed, repeated motion, and dynamic contrast can suggest storm energy.
pieces.canonicalTitle: The Four Seasons - Summer, third movement ('Storm')

pieces.sceneRole: Shivering footsteps and sharp wind-lines alternate inside a cold architectural frame.
pieces.teachingUse: Compare another season using different gesture and articulation rather than simply changing background colour.
pieces.canonicalTitle: The Four Seasons - Winter, first movement

pieces.sceneRole: A broad choral architecture rises in clear blocks; voices are represented as many human lines, not a single melody card.
pieces.teachingUse: Introduce large-scale vocal/choral public impact and sacred-origin context.

pieces.sceneRole: A river terrace moves in buoyant dance steps.
pieces.teachingUse: Present outdoor ceremonial entertainment and dance-derived rhythm.

pieces.sceneRole: Firework shapes unfold with brass-like fanfare gestures but no artificial explosion sound.
pieces.teachingUse: Show festive public music and strong ceremonial articulation.
pieces.canonicalTitle: Music for the Royal Fireworks - La Rejouissance

compareActivity.prompt: Is the music painting a scene, organising a dance, or marking a public occasion?
compareActivity.interaction: Place each excerpt under scene, movement, occasion, or more than one. The guide explains overlapping functions.

connections.label: The same era's craft moves from intimate pattern to theatre and public space.
The route continues toward the later eighteenth-century Classical city, where musical conversation and formal balance become the chapter focus.
Later composers also make scenes audible, but with different orchestras, forms, and nineteenth-century story worlds.

parentLayer: Do not add literal sound effects to prove programmatic meaning; the goal is attentive listening to the score.
Explain that The Four Seasons includes published sonnet associations, but verify exact excerpt-to-text mapping before writing child copy.
Handel's sacred and royal contexts should be accurate and concise.

artDirection.palette: Venetian aqua and terracotta shifting to London river blue, stone, and firework gold

expansion.futureRoomIdea: When all Four Seasons are present, create a full Seasons Cycle chapter while retaining Handel in a Public Baroque London chapter.
expansion.splitTrigger: Addition of Autumn plus more than one further Handel public work.

rooms.title: Vienna's Classical City
rooms.subtitle: Music becomes conversation: balanced phrases, surprise, variation, and clear musical roles.
rooms.openingQuestion: What makes music sound as if instruments are speaking, answering, joking, or changing an idea?
rooms.thesis: The Classical-era chapter emphasises audible conversation, proportion, contrast, surprise, and variation through Haydn and Mozart, using Vienna as a cultural hub rather than a claim that all Classical music came from one city.

era.label: Classical era
era.display: Approximately 1750-1820, overlapping the late Baroque and early Romantic transition
era.caution: Period labels are teaching tools and do not replace work-specific dates.

geography.anchor: Vienna with routes to Salzburg and Esterhaza/Eisenstadt contexts
geography.mapTreatment: The city map shows careers and patronage settings; do not imply Haydn and Mozart lived identical lives.

rooms.setting: A bright musical city with salon windows, theatre doors, garden paths, and a public square. Phrases pass between balconies like questions and answers.
narrativeArc: The guides arrive from the dense Baroque workshop and hear more separated musical gestures.
Haydn uses expectation and surprise.
Mozart turns conversation into serenade, symphony, keyboard play, and variation.
The final doorway reveals Beethoven arriving in the same city and pushing inherited forms in a new direction.
learningGoals: Hear balanced phrase and musical question/answer.
Notice surprise, contrast, and variation.
Understand a city as a network of composers, performers, patrons, theatres, and audiences.
Connect the traditional Twinkle-family tune to a distinct Mozart variation work.
rooms.soundBookMechanic: Balcony and garden hotspots alternate short phrases. The variation station keeps the base tune visually present while one selected variation changes around it.

pieces.sceneRole: A quiet salon pattern repeats until one architectural window suddenly opens wide.
pieces.teachingUse: Teach expectation and surprise without encouraging startling volume.

pieces.sceneRole: A trumpet messenger exchanges lively phrases with the city orchestra.
pieces.teachingUse: Introduce soloist/ensemble conversation and a newly prominent instrument sound.
pieces.canonicalTitle: Trumpet Concerto in E-flat major - third movement

pieces.sceneRole: A garden ensemble passes crisp opening gestures between lit arches.
pieces.teachingUse: Represent balanced energy and recognisable Classical phrase design.

pieces.sceneRole: A keyboard pavilion returns to a familiar refrain between contrasting sections.
pieces.teachingUse: Introduce rondo-like return and discuss stylised alla turca fashion in the adult layer rather than as authentic Turkish music.

pieces.sceneRole: A restless repeating accompaniment carries a darker, urgent melody through city streets.
pieces.teachingUse: Prevent the Classical room from being reduced to cheerful elegance and show emotional contrast within the style.

pieces.sceneRole: Two clean phrase paths answer one another on a keyboard staircase.
pieces.teachingUse: Give a clear, teachable example of phrase balance and development.
pieces.canonicalTitle: Piano Sonata in C major, K.545 - first movement

pieces.sceneRole: The Twinkle-family ribbon from Room 1 enters unchanged, then receives one carefully selected variation layer.
pieces.teachingUse: Make a direct knowledge bridge from familiar tune to formal variation; keep the traditional tune and Mozart work as separate objects.
pieces.canonicalTitle: Twelve Variations on 'Ah! vous dirai-je, maman,' K.265

compareActivity.prompt: What changed: loudness, instrument, rhythm, register, or the tune itself?
compareActivity.interaction: A city post office sorts musical change cards. The app does not require naming sonata form.

connections.label: Mozart K.265 transforms the familiar Ah vous dirai-je/Twinkle-family melody into a variation set.
Beethoven came to Vienna and studied with Haydn, then developed a distinctive path from the Classical tradition.
Classical clarity did not erase earlier craft; composers inherited and reworked counterpoint and pattern.

parentLayer: Use Vienna as a hub, not a total explanation for style.
Mozart Rondo alla Turca needs explicit framing as an eighteenth-century European stylisation, not Turkish traditional music.
The current app model that assigns the base Twinkle tune to Mozart should be migrated: base tune family and K.265 are separate records.
Do not turn surprise into a volume spike; preserve gentle audio policy.

artDirection.palette: ivory, spring green, pale blue, coral, restrained gold

expansion.futureRoomIdea: Split into Haydn House of Surprise and Mozart Theatre/Garden once the room exceeds one spread per composer.
expansion.splitTrigger: More than eight core works or more than two full Mozart scene types.

rooms.title: Beethoven's Door Between Two Eras
rooms.subtitle: The same city, inherited forms, and a new sense of scale, struggle, intimacy, and public voice.
rooms.openingQuestion: How can one composer use a tiny idea, a private piano pattern, or a broad communal theme to build very different worlds?
rooms.thesis: Beethoven connects Classical training and forms with increasingly expansive, dramatic, and personally charged musical possibilities. The room is a bridge, not a claim that one person changed every style alone.

era.label: Classical to early Romantic transition
era.display: Late eighteenth to early nineteenth century
era.caution: Transition is gradual and work-specific.

geography.anchor: Vienna, with a route from Bonn
geography.mapTreatment: Show migration and study route; link Haydn through a documented relationship rather than visual proximity alone.

rooms.setting: A monumental doorway joins the bright Classical city to a wider landscape. Five chambers reveal motif, private piano, slow procession, and communal scale.
narrativeArc: Beethoven enters Vienna through the Haydn connection.
A four-note idea becomes a structural engine.
Private piano works reveal hesitation, night, and intimacy.
The chapter expands toward symphony, slow public movement, and a melody associated with collective singing.
learningGoals: Hear motif as a small idea that can organise a large work.
Contrast intimate keyboard texture with symphonic scale.
Place Beethoven between overlapping era bands.
Understand direct teacher/student connection without reducing artistic development to one mentor.
rooms.soundBookMechanic: The doorway remembers one small visual motif and lets it reappear in different scales. Each chamber has one bounded sound object; no biographical narration precedes listening.

pieces.sceneRole: Four knocks illuminate a tiny motif tile, then the tile multiplies across a large wall.
pieces.teachingUse: Make motif construction concrete: short-short-short-long is an idea, not the entire movement.

pieces.sceneRole: A small desk drawer opens onto the oscillating opening figure and a map leading toward the lesser-known continuation.
pieces.teachingUse: Contrast famous opening with the existence of a fuller piece and preserve both-hands mode for expansion.

pieces.sceneRole: Triplet-like ripples move under a slow upper line in a dark chamber; the later nickname appears as a separate label.
pieces.teachingUse: Teach texture, atmosphere, and later naming without claiming Beethoven intended moonlight imagery.

pieces.sceneRole: A measured procession grows through repeating rhythm and layered entries.
pieces.teachingUse: Show sustained rhythmic character and orchestral accumulation beyond a four-note opening.

pieces.sceneRole: A simple stair-like melody gradually gathers multiple human lines in a large final chamber.
pieces.teachingUse: Connect recognisable simplicity with symphonic/choral scale and later public use, while avoiding the claim that no earlier symphony ever used voice.

compareActivity.prompt: Which idea is tiny, which texture is continuous, and which melody is designed to gather many voices?
compareActivity.interaction: The child chooses motif, texture, or gathering melody cards, then hears the relevant excerpt again.

connections.label: Beethoven studied with Haydn in Vienna and worked within genres shaped by Haydn and Mozart.
The private keyboard chamber opens toward Romantic piano miniatures and personal musical worlds.
Ode to Joy later acquired civic and ceremonial uses beyond its original symphonic setting.

parentLayer: Do not make deafness the explanation for every work. Present it as one important life context only where relevant and sourced.
Moonlight is a later nickname; the app should expose title history as a layer.
Claims about firsts in music history require careful wording and sources.
The room should not imply that Romanticism began on one date or with one work.

artDirection.palette: deep blue, stone grey, warm candle gold, widening dawn

expansion.futureRoomIdea: Create Beethoven Nature and Theatre side rooms once repertoire expands; keep this chapter focused on the era bridge.
expansion.splitTrigger: More than seven works or more than one full movement per major thesis.

rooms.title: Music Learns to Sing Without Words
rooms.subtitle: Voice-like melody moves from song to piano, violin, ceremony, and spring scene.
rooms.openingQuestion: What makes an instrument sound as if it is singing even when there are no words?
rooms.thesis: Early Romantic composers often foreground long, memorable melodic lines and characterful scenes. Schubert and Mendelssohn provide different routes from songfulness to instrumental storytelling.

era.label: Early Romantic era
era.display: Early to mid-nineteenth century
era.caution: Songful melody is one Romantic tendency, not a definition of all Romantic music.

geography.anchor: Vienna and Leipzig/Berlin routes
geography.mapTreatment: Keep Schubert and Mendelssohn in distinct city contexts; link through comparison, not assumed collaboration.

rooms.setting: A conservatory greenhouse where written words dissolve into instrumental ribbons. A stream, spring window, wedding arch, and violin balcony each reveal a different kind of singing line.
narrativeArc: The guides follow a sung line into instrumental space.
Schubert moves between devotional/lyric song and playful narrative song.
Mendelssohn shows wordless character, ceremony, and concerto conversation.
The exit asks whether melody can tell a story before a title is known.
learningGoals: Hear legato or voice-like melodic line.
Distinguish song, character piece, ceremony, and concerto contexts.
Notice accompaniment as support rather than an expendable background.
Connect early Romantic melody to later piano and orchestral rooms.
rooms.soundBookMechanic: A glowing breath ribbon traces the main line while support layers remain visible. The child can briefly mute the guide visual, not the accompaniment itself.

pieces.sceneRole: A long arching line moves through a quiet interior with text/sacred context held in the adult drawer.
pieces.teachingUse: Introduce sustained lyric line and the relationship between composed song and later public familiarity.

pieces.sceneRole: A quick stream line darts around a fish shadow while phrase changes follow the song story.
pieces.teachingUse: Show playful, descriptive song character and agile accompaniment.

pieces.sceneRole: A ceremonial arch advances in broad, balanced steps.
pieces.teachingUse: Connect composed theatre music with later social ceremony, keeping original context separate from later use.

pieces.sceneRole: A window opens in short, light phrases like a wordless seasonal scene.
pieces.teachingUse: Introduce the idea of a piano character piece/song without words.

pieces.sceneRole: A violin line enters almost immediately from a balcony and continues over orchestral support.
pieces.teachingUse: Show solo voice and ensemble relationship without a long orchestral introduction.
pieces.canonicalTitle: Violin Concerto in E minor - opening

compareActivity.prompt: Which line sounds like a voice, a stream, a procession, or a solo speaker?
compareActivity.interaction: Choose a motion metaphor, then compare the actual contour and rhythm; metaphors are invitations, not factual programme claims.

connections.label: Schubert worked in Beethoven's Vienna but developed a distinctive song-centred identity.
The singing line moves inward into piano miniatures, moods, memories, and named character scenes.
Wordless character and scene-painting become even more explicit in Grieg and Saint-Saens.

parentLayer: Ave Maria has text and sacred context; presentation should not imply the familiar title exhausts the work's literary history.
Wedding March later use must be separated from its original theatrical context.
Do not equate legato with emotion automatically; give one concrete audible cue.

artDirection.palette: glasshouse green, pale rose, river silver, ceremonial ivory
avoid: angel imagery as default for Ave Maria

expansion.futureRoomIdea: Split Schubert Song House from Mendelssohn Wordless/Theatre Garden when each has four or more core works.
expansion.splitTrigger: More than seven works or addition of multiple vocal text-dependent songs.

rooms.title: The Piano Diary
rooms.subtitle: One instrument can whisper, dance, remember, storm, and imagine another place.
rooms.openingQuestion: How can a short piano piece feel like a private page, a scene, or a whole emotional weather system?
rooms.thesis: Romantic piano miniatures often create concentrated worlds through texture, rhythm, register, harmony, and suggestive titles. Chopin and Schumann show different kinds of inward and characterful writing.

era.label: Romantic era
era.display: Nineteenth-century salon and domestic piano culture
era.caution: Titles and later nicknames guide listening but do not prescribe one correct feeling.

geography.anchor: Paris, Leipzig, and European salon networks
geography.mapTreatment: Show Chopin's Polish/French life context and Schumann's German context without turning nationality into a sound formula.

rooms.setting: A large illustrated diary opens into seven miniature paper worlds: moonlit room, spinning dance, rain window, rushing ink, dream page, farm scene, and imagined distant land.
narrativeArc: The guides shrink into a piano diary after the singing-line chapter.
Chopin reveals night, dance, recurring drops, and virtuoso flow.
Schumann turns childhood and imagination into compact character pages.
The child compares title, audible cue, and personal response.
learningGoals: Hear texture-dependent piano identity.
Distinguish title, nickname, and audible evidence.
Compare dance rhythm, repeated-note image, fast figuration, and lyrical miniature.
Understand why some pieces require both hands or multiple tracks in the app.
rooms.soundBookMechanic: Each diary page is a sound scene with a Famous Passage button and, where feasible, a Full Piece tab. Texture layers are preserved; melody-only playback is disabled for marked works.

pieces.sceneRole: A curved upper line floats over a patterned night accompaniment.
pieces.teachingUse: Teach ornamented songfulness and accompaniment texture; multi-track excerpt required.
pieces.canonicalTitle: Nocturne in E-flat major, Op. 9 No. 2

pieces.sceneRole: A small circular dance chases its own tail around the page.
pieces.teachingUse: Introduce fast waltz motion while the parent drawer clarifies the nickname does not mean exactly sixty seconds.

pieces.sceneRole: A recurring note appears like a mark on the window while harmony and intensity change around it.
